clue.text: Time to get stuck into romance like a Jackie Collins novel — a basic skill you'll need

indicators.note: to get stuck into tells us the time letter is pushed inside the word for romance

parts.note: to romance is to tell fanciful stories, to lie
Jackie Collins wrote steamy bestsellers, so her novels are racy

explanation.surface: A tip that a raunchy bestseller is where you pick up the basics of reading.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Romance' here is a verb meaning to fabricate a tale; T goes inside it to give LITE, and Jackie Collins, a writer of sexy blockbusters, supplies RACY.
explanation.definitionFit: Being able to read and write is the fundamental skill everyone is expected to acquire.

clue.text: Allow to make off up M1 with one's sweetheart

parts.note: to leg it is slang for running away, making off

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the letters are read from the bottom, so backwards

parts.note: the motorway name taken as its own letters
one's is a contraction of one is, giving I and S
the heart of the word sweet is its middle letter, a common crossword trick

explanation.surface: Someone is allowed to run off up Britain's main motorway with their lover.
explanation.walkthrough: The M1 is Britain's main north–south motorway; 'up' turns its letters in this down entry. 'Sweetheart' looks like a lover but means the heart of 'sweet', E.
explanation.definitionFit: To legitimise something is to make it lawful, to authorise or permit it.

clue.text: They cover me in seconds, beneath Jack

indicators.note: in a down clue, beneath puts the following piece below the sailor, so after it

parts.note: a jack tar, or jack, is an old name for a sailor
the setter of this puzzle is Paul, so me is his name

explanation.surface: Someone is wrapped up in a moment's time under a sailor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Me' is the setter speaking: Paul set this puzzle. Jack and tar are both old slang for a sailor.
explanation.definitionFit: Tarpaulins are waterproof sheets used to cover goods, boats or loads.

clue.text: Puzzling when ladder rocks (bottom sawn off)

parts.note: a ladder in a stocking is a run

indicators.note: in a down entry the bottom is the last letter, which is cut away

parts.note: ice in a drink is rocks, as in whisky on the rocks

explanation.surface: A ladder collapses after its base has been sawn through, which is baffling.
explanation.walkthrough: A ladder in tights is a RUN; drinks served 'on the rocks' come with ICE, and 'bottom sawn off' drops its last letter to leave IC.
explanation.definitionFit: Runic means written in runes, hence cryptic or mysterious in meaning.

clue.text: Consistent remark about a biscuit almost raised a point

indicators.note: about says the remark goes round the other pieces

parts.note: a remark is a comment

indicators.note: in a down clue, raised means the piece is read upwards, so backwards
almost means the last letter of the biscuit is dropped

parts.note: a rusk is a hard dry biscuit
E, east, is a point of the compass

explanation.surface: A remark about a nearly finished biscuit being lifted makes a fair point.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Raised' turns A plus RUS (the biscuit cut short by 'almost') into SURA. 'Consistent' looks like it describes the remark but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Commensurate means in proportion or corresponding, so consistent with something else.

clue.text: Shun Dutch artist, having replaced king with wife

indicators.note: having replaced ... with signals that one letter is swapped for another

parts.note: M. C. Escher was a Dutch graphic artist
R is short for rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: Someone avoids a Dutch painter, swapping the king in a picture for a wife.
explanation.walkthrough: In ESCHER the R (rex, king) is replaced, as the word 'with' completes, by W for wife.
explanation.definitionFit: To eschew is to deliberately avoid or abstain from something.

clue.text: Hole in Amundsen's equipment gets dug

indicators.note: in says the hole goes inside the explorer's gear

parts.note: Roald Amundsen, the polar explorer, travelled by sled
a hole is a squalid dwelling, a hovel

explanation.surface: A gap appears in the polar explorer's kit, and it is excavated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hole' looks literal but means a wretched little place to live, HOVEL; Amundsen, first to the South Pole, used a SLED.
explanation.definitionFit: Shovelled means moved earth with a spade, so dug.

clue.text: Man welcomes in extremists? It's not clear

indicators.note: welcomes in says the man takes the other letters inside himself

parts.note: he is the pronoun for a man
A and Z are the extremes of the alphabet

explanation.surface: A man lets radicals into his home, and the reasons are murky.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extremists' are the alphabet's end letters, A and Z, not political radicals.
explanation.definitionFit: A haze is a mist or vagueness, something that is not clear.

clue.text: Play, for example, or not!

definitions.meaning: a play is a ... of drama, an example of a creative ...
or not reads as the opposite of play, which is labour

explanation.surface: A playful quip on whether a stage piece counts as play or the opposite.
explanation.definitionFit: A play is a literary work, while work is also the opposite of play.

clue.text: Brave leader returns child buried in earth

indicators.note: buried in says the reversed child is placed inside the word for earth

parts.note: geo- is the prefix for earth

indicators.note: returns means the word is read backwards

parts.note: a minor is a child in law

explanation.surface: A tribal chief brings back a child who was buried in the ground.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'Brave' is a Native American warrior; GEO (earth, as in geology) holds MINOR reversed, RONIM.
explanation.definitionFit: Geronimo was an Apache leader, famous for resisting US forces.

clue.text: Dame Edna Everage's excellent bronze bust

indicators.note: bust means broken, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Barry Humphries' character admires a fine bronze sculpture of a head.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bust' looks like a sculpture but is the anagram signal; Dame Edna Everage is Barry Humphries' Australian comic character, hence Australian slang.
explanation.definitionFit: Bonzer is Australian slang meaning excellent, the kind of word Dame Edna would use.

clue.text: Get up one's nose? I do, with hair never old-fashioned

indicators.note: fashioned means shaped anew, so the remaining letters are rearranged
never with old says no O at all may remain in the letters

parts.note: O is the abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: Does it irritate you? I do, with my hair never in a dated style.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Never old' removes every O from ONES NOSE I DO HAIR, leaving NESNSEIDHAIR, which 'fashioned' rearranges. 'Get up one's nose' is a British idiom for annoy.
explanation.definitionFit: Rise and shine is the cheery call to get out of bed, to get up.

clue.text: Old blue bird protects newborn chick perhaps, close to snake

indicators.note: protects says the bird wraps around the other piece

parts.note: a tit is a small bird
a newly hatched chick is one that hatches, a hatcher

indicators.note: close to a word is its last letter

explanation.surface: An elderly blue bird shelters its fresh chick from a nearby snake.
explanation.walkthrough: Blue is the colour of Britain's Conservatives, so an 'Old blue' is a Tory of the 1980s Margaret Thatcher era.
explanation.definitionFit: A Thatcherite supported Margaret Thatcher, a Conservative, blue being the party colour.

clue.text: Unfair claiming giro, rat on a suspect

indicators.note: suspect as an adjective means dodgy, so the letters are unreliable and rearranged

explanation.surface: A benefits cheat's payment is reported by a dodgy informer.
explanation.walkthrough: A giro is a British state benefit cheque; 'rat on' looks like informing but is all fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Arrogation is the act of claiming or seizing something without right.

clue.text: On the other hand, he's just as good

definitions.text: On the other hand, he's just as good

parts.words: On the other hand, he's just as good
parts.note: a person equally capable with the left hand as the right one, read literally as good on either hand

explanation.definitionFit: An ambidexter is a person able to use both hands equally well.

clue.text: They can ruin your lawn, the buggers!

definitions.meaning: small burrowing mammals throw up mounds of earth on lawns
spies who plant listening bugs, agents inside an organisation

explanation.surface: A gardener's curse at the creatures digging up the grass.
explanation.definitionFit: Moles are burrowing animals and also undercover spies who may plant bugs.

clue.text: Rudder support, harsh job

parts.note: stern means strict or harsh
a post is a job or position

explanation.surface: Holding the rudder steady is a tough job.
explanation.definitionFit: A sternpost is the upright timber at a ship's stern to which the rudder is hung.

clue.text: Instrument taking horse round lake to drink

indicators.note: round says the horse goes around the lake letter

parts.note: a steed is a horse
rum is an alcoholic drink

explanation.surface: A rider leads a horse round a lake to drink with some music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drink' looks like a verb for the horse but is the noun RUM.
explanation.definitionFit: A steel drum is a Caribbean percussion instrument made from an oil drum.

clue.text: Rational to keep hospital doctor in Jewish council

indicators.note: to keep says the rational word holds the hospital letter

parts.note: sane means rational

explanation.surface: A sensible plan to keep a hospital doctor working within a religious body.
explanation.definitionFit: The Sanhedrin was the supreme council and court of ancient Israel.

clue.text: To set about wearing half of Gandhi's clothing

indicators.note: wearing says the turned word is put on, inside the half name
half of takes the second half of the letters of the name
set about means the short word is turned round

explanation.surface: Getting dressed in half of Gandhi's simple garments.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gandhi's clothing' reads as one phrase, but Gandhi only supplies the letters; the dhoti was indeed his famous garment. 'Set about' turns TO into OT.
explanation.definitionFit: A dhoti is a loincloth worn by Hindu men, famously by Gandhi.

clue.text: Nothing dissimilar to …

definitions.meaning: a British slang phrase meaning nothing at all
unlike the following clue's answer, a frankfurter in a bun, read literally

explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis leads into the next across clue: the answer is literally 'not like' a sausage, in contrast with the hot-dog answer it introduces.
explanation.definitionFit: Not a sausage is British slang for nothing whatsoever.

clue.text: Widely accepted bunch of racketeers harbouring right extremist

parts.note: U stands for universal, the film rating for all audiences

indicators.note: harbouring says the racketeers' body holds the right letter

parts.note: the LTA, Lawn Tennis Association, is a body of racket players

explanation.surface: A gang of criminals hides a far-right fanatic who is widely accepted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Racketeers' are tennis players wielding rackets, so the LTA, Britain's Lawn Tennis Association; U is the 'universal' film certificate.
explanation.definitionFit: An ultra is a person with extreme views, an extremist.

clue.text: Biblical son uniting female and male

parts.note: she is the female pronoun

explanation.surface: A scriptural son unites a woman and a man.
explanation.definitionFit: Shem was one of Noah's three sons in Genesis.

clue.text: Not all came to nursery school

indicators.note: Not all says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Not every child came along to the nursery school.
explanation.definitionFit: Eton is a famous English public school near Windsor.

clue.text: … such pants taken down smothered in ketchup and mustard?

definitions.text: … such pants taken down smothered in ketchup and mustard?

parts.words: … such pants taken down smothered in ketchup and mustard?
parts.note: a dog that is overheated pants, and a frankfurter in a bun is eaten with sauces

explanation.walkthrough: 'Pants' looks like trousers being dropped but is the verb: an overheated dog pants. 'Taken down' means eaten.
explanation.definitionFit: A hot dog is a sausage in a bun, and also an overheated, panting dog.

clue.text: Area where campaigner against land mines put her foot down

parts.note: Diana, Princess of Wales, campaigned against land mines; Di is her nickname
to put your foot down is to be strict

explanation.surface: Where the activist against mines insisted firmly on rules.
explanation.walkthrough: Princess Diana famously walked through a minefield in Angola in 1997; 'put her foot down' is an apt pun on that.
explanation.definitionFit: A district is a region or area of a country or town.

clue.text: Time light years away, stars appear so?

definitions.meaning: sixty seconds, a unit of time

definitions.text: light years away, stars appear so?
definitions.meaning: stars so distant look very tiny

explanation.surface: Gazing at faraway stars and pondering how small they look across time.
explanation.definitionFit: A minute is a unit of time; minute, said differently, means very small.

clue.text: Part-timers kept in check by Queen's servant

indicators.note: kept in says the part-timers go inside the check

parts.note: to rein is to check or restrain
the TA, Territorial Army, is Britain's part-time volunteer force
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the Queen

explanation.surface: Weekend soldiers held in line by the Queen's attendant.
explanation.walkthrough: The TA was Britain's reserve army of part-time soldiers; ER is the Queen's royal cipher.
explanation.definitionFit: A retainer is a servant or attendant kept by a household.
